terms.meaning: A way of thinking that welcomes curiosity, asks questions and stays open to the unknown. It is more than a list of facts.
Physics, chemistry, biology and earth sciences. They appear as separate chapters but are all connected.
A world where human activity does not harm the natural world that we depend on. Science can help tackle environmental challenges.

items.name: Asking deeper questions
items.formula: Ask how things work, why events happen, and what the patterns in nature teach us.
items.example: Not only "does ice melt?" but "why does it melt faster in a warm room?"

items.name: Learning by doing
items.formula: Step outside the book: activities and experiments lead to deeper understanding.
items.example: Testing which materials light a lamp teaches more than reading a list of them.

items.name: Question the answer
items.formula: Good scientists also ask interesting questions. Practise by inventing a question for a given answer.
items.example: Answer: "Just make it half." Question: "How do two friends share one cake equally?"

items.name: Big ideas from simple observations
items.formula: Careful watching of simple things can lead to real inventions.
items.example: Studying bird wings and paper planes led towards designing aircraft.

items.name: One idea leads to another
items.formula: An idea in one field often inspires discoveries or questions in another.
items.example: Shadows lead to telling the time, and the shadows of the Earth and Moon lead to eclipses.

items.name: Science and responsibility
items.formula: Discovery comes with responsibility, because human activities are linked to the natural world and to society.
items.example: Learning how factory waste harms a lake also tells us to treat the waste first.

mistakes.text: Science is not only memorising facts. Asking questions and testing them is science too.
Physics, chemistry and biology are not separate worlds. Ideas move between them.
